config.title: Pagination

intro.title: Pagination
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple pagination component that splits a list of items into manageable pages. You will learn how to track the current page, calculate the total number of pages, and navigate between them. The core programming concept involves using component state to manage the current page index and performing calculations to slice the data array. You will use Angular's built-in directives and TypeScript to create a reusable, interactive pagination feature for your applications.
intro.usecase: Pagination is essential for managing large datasets in real-world applications where displaying all content at once would overwhelm users and degrade performance. You'll implement pagination in e-commerce product listings, search engine results, and admin dashboards showing user records or transaction histories. As an Angular developer, you'll create paginated tables for data-heavy enterprise applications, news/article feeds, and social media platforms where users need to navigate through content efficiently. This pattern improves user experience by breaking information into manageable chunks while maintaining application responsiveness.

objectives: Construct a pagination component with Angular's component decorator
Initialize and manage pagination state using reactive properties
Implement page navigation controls with click event handlers
Configure dynamic page number generation based on data length
Bind pagination controls to display and update current page status
Integrate pagination logic with a data service to fetch page-specific results
Render paginated data in a template using Angular's structural directives

steps.title: Import Angular core and necessary modules
steps.instruction: Import Component and OnInit from '@angular/core', and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.
steps.hint: Use the import keyword followed by curly braces to import specific symbols from their module packages.
steps.seedCode: // Import Component and OnInit from '@angular/core', and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary Angular modules are imported, enabling component creation and template directives.
successCriteria: Component and OnInit are imported from '@angular/core', and CommonModule is imported from '@angular/common'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've imported all three required items: Component, OnInit, and CommonModule from their correct module paths.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. Remember to import Component and OnInit from '@angular/core', and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.

steps.title: Create the PaginationComponent class
steps.instruction: Define the PaginationComponent class with the @Component decorator and implement the OnInit interface.
steps.hint: Use the class keyword, add @Component decorator with a selector and template, and implement OnInit.
steps.expectedOutcome: A basic Angular component class is created with proper TypeScript structure.
successCriteria: PaginationComponent class is defined with @Component decorator and implements OnInit.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both the @Component decorator and the class implementing OnInit.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component class isn't properly defined. Check that you have the @Component decorator and class definition.

steps.title: Define component metadata and template
steps.instruction: Add the @Component decorator above your class with selector 'app-pagination' and an empty template string.
steps.hint: Use @Component({ selector: 'app-pagination', template: '' }) right before the class declaration.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have proper Angular metadata with a selector and empty template.
successCriteria: Component has @Component decorator with selector 'app-pagination' and empty template property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've configured the component metadata correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both selector and template properties in the @Component decorator.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you added the @Component decorator with the correct selector and template.

steps.title: Initialize pagination state properties
steps.instruction: Inside the PaginationComponent class, add three public properties: currentPage (number), itemsPerPage (number), and totalItems (number). Initialize them with default values (e.g., 1, 10, 100).
steps.hint: Use TypeScript type annotations (e.g., currentPage: number = 1) to define typed properties directly in the class.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has typed state variables to manage pagination logic.
successCriteria: The PaginationComponent class contains currentPage, itemsPerPage, and totalItems properties with number types and initial values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some properties, but make sure all three (currentPage, itemsPerPage, totalItems) are present with number types and initial values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The pagination state properties are missing or incorrect. Add currentPage, itemsPerPage, and totalItems as typed number properties with default values.

steps.title: Add total pages calculation
steps.instruction: In the PaginationComponent class, add a getter method named totalPages that calculates the total number of pages based on totalItems and itemsPerPage.
steps.hint: Use a getter method with the 'get' keyword. The calculation should divide totalItems by itemsPerPage and round up using Math.ceil().
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a computed property that calculates total pages from totalItems and itemsPerPage.
successCriteria: A getter method named totalPages is added to the PaginationComponent class, correctly calculating total pages using Math.ceil().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a method, but check if it's a getter (using the 'get' keyword) and if it correctly uses Math.ceil() to round up the division result.
steps.feedbackWrong: The totalPages getter method is missing or incorrect. Make sure to add a getter method that calculates Math.ceil(totalItems / itemsPerPage).

steps.title: Add initial template structure
steps.instruction: Inside the @Component decorator's template property, create a <nav> element with an unordered list (<ul>) for pagination buttons.
steps.hint: The template should start with a <nav> tag containing a <ul> element. This will serve as the container for your pagination controls.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component template now has a basic navigation structure ready to hold pagination buttons.
successCriteria: The @Component decorator's template property contains a <nav> element with a <ul> element inside it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added both the <nav> element and the <ul> element inside it within the template property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template structure isn't quite right. You need to add a <nav> element containing a <ul> element inside the template property of the @Component decorator.

steps.title: Implement previous button
steps.instruction: Inside the template, add a button element for navigating to the previous page. Use Angular event binding to call the goToPage method when clicked, passing the current page minus one. Add a disabled attribute that binds to a condition checking if the current page is the first page.
steps.hint: Use (click) event binding to call goToPage(currentPage - 1). The disabled attribute can use property binding like [disabled]="currentPage === 1".
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: Previous button with event binding and disabled state
<button (click)="goToPage(currentPage - 1)" [disabled]="currentPage === 1">Previous</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The template should now contain a previous button that triggers page navigation and is disabled on the first page.
successCriteria: A button element with (click) event binding to goToPage(currentPage - 1) and [disabled] property binding checking if currentPage === 1 is added to the template.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but check if it has both the click event binding and disabled property binding correctly implemented.
steps.feedbackWrong: The previous button is missing or doesn't have the required event binding and disabled state logic.

steps.title: Add page number buttons
steps.instruction: In the component's template, add a <button> element for each page number using *ngFor to iterate from 1 to totalPages. Each button should display the page number and call goToPage(page) when clicked.
steps.hint: Use *ngFor="let page of [1,2,3,...,totalPages]" to generate the buttons. You'll need to create an array of page numbers in your component logic first.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: generating buttons for items
<button *ngFor="let item of items" (click)="selectItem(item)">{{ item }}</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a method to generate page numbers and the template will display clickable page buttons using *ngFor.
successCriteria: Template contains *ngFor loop generating buttons with page numbers and (click) event handlers calling goToPage().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure each button displays the page number and has a click handler that calls goToPage() with the correct page.
steps.feedbackWrong: The page buttons aren't properly implemented. Check that you're using *ngFor to generate buttons for each page and wiring the click events correctly.

steps.title: Implement next button
steps.instruction: Add a next button to the template that calls goToPage() with currentPage + 1 when clicked and is disabled when currentPage equals totalPages.
steps.hint: Use a button element with (click) event binding and [disabled] property binding. The click handler should pass currentPage + 1 to goToPage().
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will have a next button that increments the current page when clicked and becomes disabled on the last page.
successCriteria: A button element with (click)="goToPage(currentPage + 1)" and [disabled]="currentPage === totalPages" is added to the template.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but check the click handler or disabled condition. The button should call goToPage(currentPage + 1) and disable when currentPage equals totalPages.
steps.feedbackWrong: The next button is missing or incorrect. Add a button with (click)="goToPage(currentPage + 1)" and [disabled]="currentPage === totalPages".
